Analysis · Europe

European Accessibility Act: what changes for private companies

Published on 27 October 2026Reading time: 8 minutesBy the firm’s team

EAADirective (EU) 2019/882
Applicable since 28 June 2025

Contents

  1. What the European Accessibility Act is
  2. Products and services covered
  3. Who is exempt?
  4. Transition periods
  5. What you need to do in practice
  6. Country by country

Since 28 June 2025, digital accessibility is no longer just a matter for the public sector. With the European Accessibility Act, many private companies that sell to consumers must make their products and services usable by people with disabilities.

What the European Accessibility Act is

The European Accessibility Act is Directive (EU) 2019/882 of 17 April 2019. It sets common accessibility requirements across the Union for a list of products and services, so that companies no longer have to deal with different rules from one country to another.

Each Member State has transposed it into national law. The new rules have applied since 28 June 2025, with checks carried out by each country’s market surveillance authorities.

Products and services covered

The text first covers products, and above all their digital interfaces:

  • computers and their operating systems;
  • payment terminals, cash machines, check-in and ticketing kiosks;
  • smartphones and communication equipment;
  • equipment giving access to audiovisual media services;
  • e-readers.

It also covers services, most of which are delivered through a website or an app:

  • e-commerce;
  • consumer banking services;
  • electronic communication services;
  • access to audiovisual media services;
  • websites, apps, e-tickets and information for passenger transport services;
  • e-books and their reading software.
Key point

An online shop selling to consumers in the European Union falls within the scope of the EAA, unless it is exempt.

Who is exempt?

Micro-enterprises providing services are exempt: fewer than 10 people, and an annual turnover or balance sheet total of no more than €2 million.

A company may also invoke a disproportionate burden or a fundamental alteration of its product or service. This exception is strictly framed: it must be assessed, documented and reviewed regularly.

Transition periods

Service providers may continue to deliver their services using products they lawfully used before 28 June 2025, until 28 June 2030. Self-service terminals already installed may remain in use until the end of their economically useful life, up to a maximum of 20 years.

These periods do not apply to new websites and apps: whatever goes live today must meet the requirements.

What you need to do in practice

  1. Map the products and services affected, country by country.
  2. Audit your websites and apps against EN 301 549, which includes WCAG level AA.
  3. Fix starting with essential journeys: search, purchase, payment, customer account.
  4. Inform your customers about how your service meets the accessibility requirements.
  5. Train your teams so that new features remain compliant.
  6. Maintain the level reached with acceptance testing at every release.

Country by country

In France, Belgium and Luxembourg, the EAA has been transposed into national law and comes on top of public-sector obligations. Switzerland is not a member of the European Union, but Swiss companies selling to European consumers are affected for those sales.

Our pages on France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland describe the framework in each country.
